title: My peace I give you (John 14:22–31)

lines: AT A GOODBYE, PEOPLE GIVE ONE THING.
cards: A ring. A recipe card. A watch.

At a hospital bed or an airport gate, when a goodbye is serious, people often skip the speech and hand over one small thing, something to hold when the person isn't there. At the last supper, Jesus knows he's leaving.
A second Judas at the table, not Iscariot, has just asked him a question. Jesus answers, and then he does what people do at goodbyes. He leaves them something.

teach.h: A GOODBYE GIFT: PEACE I LEAVE WITH YOU.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid." It's a bequest.
I leave with you: the language of someone settling what they're handing on.
The Greek word is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom, which Jews used, and still use, as a greeting and a goodbye. Shalom is more than quiet.
It carries the sense of wholeness, everything in its right place, nothing missing. So in one way this is the ordinary farewell any Jewish teacher might give his friends.
Then the strange part: not as the world giveth. How does the world give peace? Usually by removing the problem.
Pay the bill, end the argument, win the war, then relax. Jesus is about to be arrested. Nothing is being removed.
The peace he offers comes in the middle of the trouble, not after it. He also promises a helper, the Holy Ghost, who will teach them and bring to their remembrance everything he said.
Then the chapter ends with an odd line: "Arise, let us go hence."

teach.h: ARISE, LET US GO, AND HE KEEPS TALKING.
teach.b: And yet he keeps talking for three more chapters before they leave. Readers have long puzzled over that. Some think the Gospel was edited in stages; others think they rose and he went on speaking as they walked.

teach.h: MY PEACE I GIVE UNTO YOU.
teach.b: In some churches the gift comes back every week: at the passing of the peace, people turn to the person next to them and say, peace be with you.

how: In many churches, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and others, the congregation shares the peace during the service, turning to neighbors with a handshake or embrace and the words peace be with you.

o: wholeness, nothing missing, even in trouble
a calm life once every problem is gone
a truce signed once the fighting stops

games.q: what's inside John 14:22–31 — tap the pairs.

s: the Judas who asks a question here is Judas Iscariot
John says plainly it was Judas, not Iscariot.
Jesus leaves his peace as a parting gift
"Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you."
the disciples leave the room right after 'arise, let us go hence'
he keeps speaking for three more chapters. the text doesn't explain why.

games.q: you're at the table. your teacher says he's leaving, and trouble is coming. what does he hand you?
o: a plan to escape the city.
his own peace, not as the world gives.
a promise that nothing bad will happen.
games.why: he gives peace without removing the danger: "not as the world giveth, give I unto you."

practice: Notice one trouble you're carrying right now, and don't try to solve it; just let it be there, and in the middle of it, breathe slower. That's the shape of the peace in this chapter: not after the trouble, but inside it.
Then picture one person who's carrying something heavy, and if you pray, say his words for them, peace I leave with you; if not, simply wish them wholeness.

wordCard.voice: Peace. The Hebrew shalom behind Jesus's farewell gift: wholeness offered in the middle of trouble, not after it.

orig.note: Greek: peace. in the Gospels it often carries the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, well-being, a greeting and a farewell.

carryVoice: Your line: not as the world gives. Peace in the middle, not after. Day six hundred thirty-three.

sources.q: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
